subject: Mathematics
topic: Exponential growth, decay and changing time units
scope: Original digital SAT nonlinear-function and nonlinear-equation practice, checked against the official SAT Math skill table on 2026-10-19. Covers constant-factor models, not every nonlinear family or every SAT item format.
prerequisites: Convert percentages to decimals and multiply powers.
Distinguish an initial value from a rate of change.
objectives: Build and interpret a constant-factor model.
Convert a growth factor between time units.
Distinguish linear changes from exponential changes.
Check model assumptions and discrete-time restrictions.

remaining: Other nonlinear families, more graph representations and independent review.

syllabusMappings.tier: Digital SAT Math; recognisable powers and thresholds only
remaining: Broader nonlinear equation families and mixed symbolic forms.

notes.heading: Equal intervals and equal factors
paragraphs: A positive exponential model can be written P(t)=A b^t with A>0 and b>0. The variable t counts intervals of a stated duration. A is the value when t=0, while b is the multiplier for one such interval. If b>1 the quantity grows; if 0<b<1 it decays. The special value b=1 gives a constant quantity. Do not call b itself a percentage rate: b=1.08 represents an 8% increase, whereas b=0.92 represents an 8% decrease.

An exponential model has a constant ratio over equal intervals, not a constant difference. A table with values 40, 60, 90 and 135 at equal time steps has ratio 1.5. Its differences increase. A table with values 40, 60, 80 and 100 has constant difference 20 and is linear instead. Unequal time intervals require different comparisons; reading the time labels is part of the mathematics.

notes.heading: Compounding and percentage reversal
paragraphs: A percentage change applies to the current amount. After two increases of r expressed as a decimal, the factor is (1+r)², not 1+2r. Similarly, a reduction by r gives factor 1-r. An increase followed by an equal percentage decrease has factor (1+r)(1-r)=1-r², so it does not return to the original amount unless r=0. This happens because the second percentage uses a different base.

To undo a multiplicative change, divide by its factor. A 20% reduction leaves factor 0.8; returning to the starting value requires multiplication by 1/0.8=1.25, which is a 25% increase from the reduced amount. State the reference quantity whenever you interpret a percentage. These are hypothetical numerical models, not predictions or recommendations about financial products.

notes.heading: Changing the time unit
paragraphs: If an annual multiplier is b and t is measured in months, use b^(t/12), equivalently (b^(1/12))^t. The monthly multiplier is the twelfth root of the annual multiplier under the constant-factor model. Dividing the annual percentage rate by 12 is generally only an approximation and does not preserve exact compounding. Conversely, a factor g per month gives g^12 per year.

A model A b^(t/k) applies one factor b every k units of t. To interpret it, first identify the unit of t and the meaning of k. For a quantity halving every five hours, P(t)=A(1/2)^(t/5). At ten hours the exponent is 2, so one quarter remains. Fractional exponents interpolate continuously; if the actual process updates only at fixed events, that interpolation is a modelling assumption rather than a directly observed state.

notes.heading: Recovering parameters and thresholds
paragraphs: Two positive observations can determine A and b once the time origin and interval length are fixed. Divide the later quantity by the earlier quantity to cancel A, then account for the number of intervals separating them. If P(2)=72 and P(5)=243, then b³=243/72=27/8, so b=3/2, and A=72/(3/2)²=32. Substitution into both observations checks both parameters.

Some equations can be solved by recognising powers, such as 3^t=81. More general equations may require logarithms or a graph, but those procedures are not the focus of this lesson. For a threshold in a discrete process, do not report a fractional update count. Check the neighbouring integers and choose the first that satisfies the actual inequality. A strict condition such as exceeding 100 differs from reaching at least 100.

notes.heading: Graph shape and model limits
paragraphs: For A>0 and b>0, the model A b^t remains positive for every real t and has vertical intercept A. A decay curve approaches zero without reaching it at a finite time in this model. Real objects may be counted in whole units or disappear at a detection threshold, so that mathematical behaviour is not always literal. Adding a constant offset changes the horizontal asymptote and means the raw output ratios need not be constant.

Constant-rate models often describe only a limited interval. Resource limits, changing conditions and measurement error can make long-range extrapolation unreliable. Fit and prediction are different claims: agreement with a few data points does not establish that the same multiplier will hold indefinitely. Preserve the model's domain and give units with any interpretation of A or t.

notes.heading: Revision checks and syllabus scope
paragraphs: This crosswalk targets selected digital SAT skills about nonlinear relationships and equations. It does not substitute for practice on rational, radical, absolute-value or other nonlinear forms. The official source is a dated live specification table, not a claimed immutable examination-year edition. The questions here are original teaching exercises with editorial marking points, not reproduced SAT questions.

When revising, identify the initial value, multiplier and time unit before touching a calculator. Estimate whether the answer should be above or below the initial value. Check results by substituting them into the original model and by comparing adjacent time points. Keep the distinction between a numerical value matching a practice key and a justified interpretation of the model.

notes.heading: Reversing a percentage change with a reciprocal factor
paragraphs: A percentage change acts on the current quantity. After a decrease, an equal percentage increase uses a smaller base and therefore does not generally restore the original value. Represent each change as a multiplier and compose the multipliers in order. To reverse a decrease by a factor r, use the reciprocal multiplier 1/r, provided r is positive. The restoring percentage increase is then (1/r - 1) times 100%. This is arithmetic within a fictional model, not a forecast. A repeated-growth interpretation also requires equal time intervals and a constant factor; the percentage rule alone does not establish that those assumptions hold in real data.

notes.heading: Compare factors over the same interval
paragraphs: A growth factor belongs to a time interval. A two-year factor cannot be used once per year without changing the model. To recover a factor for a shorter interval, use a root under the assumption of uniform exponential change. A percentage decrease can also be reversed only relative to the reduced value; it does not have the same denominator as the original change. For inequalities, consider whether the factor is above or below one before interpreting logarithms or integer thresholds. Check the neighbouring integer to confirm the first or last qualifying interval.

workedExamples.prompt: A model starts at 500 units and decreases by 12% each day. Find its value after two days.
A population model triples every four days. Write it for initial value 200 and t measured in days.
steps: One factor of 3 applies every four days.
The number of four-day periods is t/4.
Check t=0 gives 200 and t=4 gives 600.

workedExamples.prompt: For A b^t, P(1)=30 and P(3)=120. Find A and b, with b>0.
A count model N(n)=6×2^n updates at integer n≥0. Find the first n for which N(n)>100.
steps: At n=4, N=96, which does not exceed 100.
Since the sequence increases, 5 is the first qualifying update.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional quantity starts at 250, decreases by 20%, then increases by 20%. Find the final quantity and its overall percentage change from the start.
steps: A 20% decrease multiplies 250 by 0.8 to give 200.
The next 20% increase multiplies 200 by 1.2 to give 240.
workedExamples.answer: The final quantity is 240, an overall decrease of 4%.

misconceptions.correction: The multiplier is 1.08; 0.08 describes only the added fraction.

misconceptions.claim: Equal percentage increase and decrease cancel.
misconceptions.correction: They act on different bases; the combined multiplier is generally below 1.

misconceptions.claim: A constant annual rate can always be divided by 12 exactly.
misconceptions.correction: Exact constant-factor conversion uses the twelfth root of the annual multiplier.

flashcards.front: What does A represent in A b^t?
What table feature distinguishes positive exponential change over equal intervals?
flashcards.back: A constant ratio, rather than a constant difference.

flashcards.front: How do two successive multipliers combine?
How do you undo a multiplier of 0.75?
What exponent represents doubling every six hours with t in hours?
How is monthly multiplier g converted to an annual multiplier?
What must be checked for an integer-update threshold?
flashcards.back: The neighbouring integer counts and the direction/strictness of the inequality.

flashcards.front: Does A b^t with 0<b<1 reach zero at finite t?
flashcards.back: Not in this positive exponential model.

flashcards.front: Why is extrapolation beyond fitted data uncertain?
flashcards.back: The constant-factor assumption may stop holding.

flashcards.front: Why do equal percentage decreases and increases fail to cancel?
flashcards.back: They act on different bases, so their multipliers have product below one for equal nonzero magnitudes less than 100%.

flashcards.front: How do you reverse a positive multiplier r?

questions.prompt: Which expression models an initial 80 units growing by 5% per interval?
solution: Growth retains the whole current amount and adds 5%.
The interval multiplier is 1.05.

questions.prompt: A quantity of 640 halves every three hours. What does the model predict after nine hours?
solution: Nine hours contains three halving intervals.
Compute 640×(1/2)³.

questions.prompt: A value is multiplied by 1.2 then by 0.8. Explain its net change.
questions.answer: The combined factor is 0.96, a 4% decrease from the original.
solution: Multiply 1.2×0.8.
Compare 0.96 with the original factor 1.
markingPoints: Interpret the percentage relative to the original.

questions.prompt: For a positive constant-factor model, P(0)=50 and P(2)=200. Find the multiplier per interval.
solution: Use 50b²=200.
Then b²=4 and b=2 since b>0.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between 100(1.1)^t and 100+10t even though both equal 110 at t=1.
questions.answer: The first increases by 10% of the current amount, the second by 10 units. At t=2 they give 121 and 120, so equality at one time does not imply the same model.
solution: Identify multiplicative versus additive change.
Compare at a second time.
Explain why one shared value is insufficient.

questions.prompt: For integer n≥0, N(n)=5×3^n. Find the first n at which N(n)≥400.
solution: At n=3, N=135, below 400.
At n=4, N=405; monotonic growth establishes it is first.

questions.prompt: If b is an annual multiplier, write the exact monthly multiplier under uniform exponential change.
solution: Twelve monthly factors must multiply to b.
Solve g^12=b for positive g.

questions.prompt: A model fits a microorganism count for the first four hours. Why is a fifty-hour prediction not automatically reliable?
questions.answer: The growth multiplier may change as resources, conditions or measurement regimes change. A short fitted interval does not establish indefinitely constant growth.
solution: Identify the extrapolation beyond observed times.
Explain a mechanism that could change the factor.
Limit the conclusion to the evidence.

questions.prompt: A fictional quantity starts at 250, decreases by 20%, then increases by 20%. Find the final quantity and its overall percentage change from the start.
questions.answer: The final quantity is 240, an overall decrease of 4%.
solution: A 20% decrease multiplies 250 by 0.8 to give 200.
The next 20% increase multiplies 200 by 1.2 to give 240.
The change from 250 is -10, so -10/250 × 100 = -4%.
markingPoints: A 20% decrease multiplies 250 by 0.8 to give 200.
The next 20% increase multiplies 200 by 1.2 to give 240.

questions.prompt: A learner says a 20% increase always reverses a 20% decrease. Give the actual restoring percentage and explain its denominator.
questions.answer: A 25% increase reverses a 20% decrease, because the lost 50 is 25% of the reduced value 200.
solution: After the decrease the base is 200, not 250.
The required increase is (250 - 200)/200 × 100 = 25%.
Equivalently, the restoring factor is 1/0.8 = 1.25.
markingPoints: After the decrease the base is 200, not 250.

questions.prompt: An idealised quantity rises from 200 to 242 in two years with a constant positive annual multiplier. Find that multiplier and the modelled year-one value.
solution: Solve b²=242/200=1.21 and choose the positive root.
Multiply 200 by 1.1 for one year.

questions.prompt: A model has A_n=100(1/2)^n for integer n≥0. Find the first n for which A_n<4, checking the preceding value.
solution: Evaluate the halving sequence near the threshold.
Use the strict inequality and monotonic decrease to establish the first qualifying index.

questions.prompt: A fictional price increases by 10% in each of two years. A learner calls the overall increase 20%. Find the actual increase and explain the difference.
solution: The second increase applies to the already increased value.
For an initial 100, the sequence is 100,110,121.
markingPoints: Explain the changed base for year two.
